# **some-stripe — Microkernel Rust SDK & Constant-Time Webhook Engine for Stripe**

An idiomatic, production-grade Rust SDK and cryptographic webhook verification engine for the **Stripe API** (v1 and v2), designed to mirror the ergonomics and hierarchical namespace structure of the official [stripe-node](https://github.com/stripe/stripe-node) client while enforcing strict compile-time memory safety, zero data races, and constant-time (subtle::ConstantTimeEq) signature verification1.

## **Executive Summary and Microkernel Architectural Philosophy**

Building some-stripe—an idiomatic, production-grade Rust SDK and webhook verification engine modeled after the official stripe-node client—requires bridging two fundamentally different language paradigms1. The official Node.js SDK (stripe-node v22 and v23) relies on dynamic prototype attachment, deeply nested TypeScript namespace declarations, runtime reflection for URL path interpolation, and garbage-collected promise chains1. Translating these ergonomics into Rust while enforcing strict compile-time memory safety, zero data races, and constant-time cryptographic verification demands a deliberate hybrid of OpenAPI-driven code generation and hand-crafted core runtime primitives1.  
To ensure developers can start with a lightweight, ultra-fast-compiling baseline and scale up only as their workflows grow in complexity, some-stripe is engineered around a **Microkernel Architecture**:

> 1. **The Microkernel Core (some-stripe-core / default minimal install):** Provides the thread-safe StripeClient (Arc\<ClientInner\>), the pluggable HttpClient transport trait, per-request RequestOptions (idempotency keys, Stripe-Account multi-tenancy, retries), the dual-protocol serializer (application/x-www-form-urlencoded with indexed brackets for API v1 and application/json for API v2), polymorphic Expandable\<T\> and Nullable\<T\> primitives, the Paginator\<T\> async stream engine, and raw request execution2.  
> 2. **Opt-In Domain Plugins (Cargo Feature Flags):** Because compiling the entirety of Stripe's massive surface area—spanning 38 root resource services, 18 specialized product namespaces, and API v2 endpoints—into a single monolithic compilation unit severely degrades build performance, every service domain is isolated as a modular plugin mounted onto the microkernel via Cargo feature flags3.  
> 3. **Standalone or Integrated Webhook Engine (webhooks feature / some-stripe-webhooks):** Provides zero-allocation HMAC-SHA256 verification and strongly-typed event parsing that can run independently in edge/serverless functions without compiling the HTTP transport layer4.

A critical architectural inflection point in the Stripe ecosystem is the coexistence of **API v1** and **API v2**1. While API v1 encompasses the vast majority of legacy and current merchant workflows—relying on application/x-www-form-urlencoded request bodies, bracketed query serialization, and cursor-based has\_more pagination—API v2 introduces JSON-native request payloads, URL-driven cursor pagination (next\_page\_url and previous\_page\_url), operation-specific parameter schemas, and thin event notifications6. In official SDKs such as stripe-java and stripe-node, top-level client accessors are increasingly partitioned to distinguish v1 namespaces from v2 namespaces (client.v2.core.\*), making dual-protocol support a mandatory baseline requirement for the some-stripe microkernel6.

## **Progressive Feature Flag Matrix & Quick Start Workflows**

With the microkernel design, users only compile and pay for the exact Stripe workflows their application requires8.

### **1\. Minimal Microkernel Installation (Cargo.toml)**

Start with just the microkernel runtime, basic payment intents, and constant-time webhook verification3:

Ini, TOML  
\[dependencies\]  
some-stripe \= { version \= "0.1", default-features \= false, features \= \[  
    "rt-tokio-hyper", \# Pluggable HTTP transport (or use custom/WASM fetch client)  
    "payments",       \# Core PaymentIntents, SetupIntents, Charges, Refunds  
    "webhooks",       \# Constant-time Stripe-Signature HMAC-SHA256 verification  
\] }

### **3\. Ergonomic Usage Examples (stripe-node Style in Rust)**

Rust  
use some\_stripe::{StripeClient, RequestOptions};  
use some\_stripe::checkout::SessionCreateParams;

\#\[tokio::main\]  
async fn main() \-\> Result\<(), some\_stripe::StripeError\> {  
    // 1\. Initialize the thread-safe Microkernel Client (cheaply cloneable via Arc)  
    let stripe \= StripeClient::builder("sk\_test\_51...")  
        .max\_network\_retries(2)  
        .build()?;

    // 2\. Call mounted service plugins using stripe-node style chaining  
    let session \= stripe  
        .checkout()  
        .sessions()  
        .create(SessionCreateParams {  
            mode: Some(some\_stripe::checkout::SessionMode::Subscription),  
            success\_url: Some("https\://example.com/success".into()),  
            ..Default::default()  
        })  
        .options(  
            RequestOptions::new()  
                .stripe\_account("acct\_12345")  
                .idempotency\_key("idem\_checkout\_98765"),  
        )  
        .await?;

    println\!("Created Checkout Session: {}", session.id);

    // 3\. Auto-paginate seamlessly across V1 or V2 endpoints  
    let mut customers \= stripe.customers().list(Default::default()).paginate();  
    while let Some(customer) \= customers.next\_item().await? {  
        println\!("Customer: {:?}", customer.id);  
    }

    Ok(())  
}

## **Core Microkernel Runtime Architecture: Translating stripe-node to Idiomatic Rust**

### **Client Instantiation, Thread Safety, and Request Options**

In stripe-node v22 and v23, the legacy factory function Stripe('sk\_test\_...') was deprecated and replaced by strict ES6 class instantiation (new Stripe('sk\_test\_...', config)), where host overrides and network configurations are bound immutably to the client instance rather than mutated via setter methods2. In some-stripe, the top-level StripeClient microkernel struct encapsulates an Arc\<ClientInner\> so that cloning the client across asynchronous Tokio tasks or Axum and Actix-web request handlers is a cheap, lock-free pointer copy that guarantees Send, Sync, and zero data races3. Domain plugins are attached as zero-cost wrapper structs borrowing \&StripeClient via extension traits or feature-gated methods, incurring zero runtime memory overhead when unused8.  
Every service method in stripe-node accepts up to three positional layers: required resource identifiers (such as cus\_123), an optional operation-specific parameter object, and a trailing RequestOptions structure2. While stripe-node v22 removed support for per-request host overrides and raw string API key arguments, it standardized RequestOptions as the vehicle for per-request execution context2.

| stripe-node Configuration / Option | Scope | HTTP / Runtime Mapping | Idiomatic some-stripe Rust Representation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| apiKey | Client & Per-Request | Authorization: Bearer \<key\> | SecretString (zeroized on drop; prevents Debug leakage)2 |
| stripeAccount | Client & Per-Request | Stripe-Account: \<acct\_id\> | Option\<AccountId\> for Connect multi-tenancy2 |
| stripeContext | Client & Per-Request | Stripe-Context: \<ctx\> | Option\<StripeContext\> (replaces StripeContext type export in v22)2 |
| idempotencyKey | Per-Request | Idempotency-Key: \<uuid\> | Option\<String\> (auto-generated UUID v4 on safe retries)3 |
| apiVersion | Client & Per-Request | Stripe-Version: \<version\> | Pinned compile-time constant (e.g., "2025-06-30.basil") with override12 |
| maxNetworkRetries | Client & Per-Request | Retry loop controller | u8 (defaults to 1 or 2 with jittered exponential backoff)12 |
| timeout | Client & Per-Request | Socket/Future timeout | std::time::Duration (applied via tokio::time::timeout)12 |
| host / port / protocol | Client-Only (v22+) | Base URI construction | url::Url (per-request host disallowed as of stripe-node v22)2 |
| httpClient | Client-Only | Pluggable transport trait | Arc\<dyn HttpClient \+ Send \+ Sync\> for mocking & WASM/Edge runtimes11 |
| STRIPE\_SUPPRESS\_NOTICES | Environment Variable | Stderr notice suppression | Checked once via std::env::var for sandbox notice suppression1 |

To avoid forcing Rust callers to pass None for RequestOptions on every API call—a point of friction noted in stripe-node v22 where callers must pass undefined explicitly when omitting parameters before RequestOptions—some-stripe employs a fluent request builder pattern in the microkernel2. Invoking client.customers().retrieve("cus\_123") returns a CustomerRetrieveRequest future builder implementing std::future::IntoFuture2. Callers can immediately .await the builder for default execution, or chain .params(params) and .options(RequestOptions::new().stripe\_account("acct\_123").idempotency\_key("...")) prior to awaiting2.

### **Dual-Protocol Serialization: V1 Form-Urlencoded vs. V2 JSON**

A common pitfall when engineering custom Stripe clients is assuming the entire REST API accepts JSON request bodies17. In **API v1**, sending Content-Type: application/json to a POST /v1/... endpoint results in an immediate HTTP 400 invalid\_request\_error stating that the POST content type must be application/x-www-form-urlencoded17. Furthermore, Stripe's v1 backend parser enforces strict syntactic rules on nested objects and arrays that standard Rust serde\_urlencoded cannot satisfy without a custom serializer3.  
Specifically, nested structs and maps (such as metadata or shipping\[address\]\[city\]) must be flattened into bracketed keys of the form parent\[child\]\[grandchild\]=value10. When serializing arrays of objects, as documented in stripe-node Issue \#561, passing unindexed brackets (subscription\_items\[\]\[id\]=si\_123\&subscription\_items\[\]\[plan\]=pro) causes parameter misattribution and range errors on Stripe's backend across both GET query strings and POST bodies10. Consequently, the custom serde::Serializer in some-stripe-core tracks sequence offsets and emits explicit zero-based integer indices for all array elements, producing subscription\_items\[0\]\[id\]=si\_123\&subscription\_items\[1\]\[plan\]=pro10.  
In addition to indexed array formatting, the v1 serializer must distinguish between omitting a parameter and explicitly clearing a field on Stripe's backend9. During an update operation, omitting a field leaves its stored value unchanged (represented in Rust by Option::None with \#\[serde(skip\_serializing\_if \= "Option::is\_none")\]), whereas setting a field or array (such as legal\_entity.additional\_owners or metadata\[key\]) to null instructs stripe-node's stringifyRequestData utility to emit an empty string (additional\_owners= or metadata\[key\]=), which clears the value on Stripe's servers9. In some-stripe-core, updatable nullable fields are modeled using a three-state generic wrapper Nullable\<T\> (with variants Value(T), Null, and Omit), where Nullable::Null serializes as ""9. Exceptions to standard form encoding occur in two places: binary file uploads (POST /v1/files routed to files.stripe.com), which require multipart/form-data, and **API v2** endpoints (/v2/...), which exclusively accept application/json payloads and utilize operation-specific nested structs (for instance, v2::core::AccountUpdateParamsIdentityIndividualAddress rather than sharing v1's AddressParam)6.

### **Type System Ergonomics: Expandable Resources and Open Enums**

Two type-system challenges dominate Stripe SDK design: polymorphic object expansion and forward-compatible enumerations8. Many Stripe endpoints accept an expand: Vec\<String\> parameter that replaces foreign-key string identifiers (such as "customer": "cus\_123" or "latest\_charge": "ch\_123") in the JSON response with the full hydrated resource object7. some-stripe-core models every expandable relationship using an untagged generic enum Expandable\<T\> annotated with \#\[serde(untagged)\], containing two variants: Id(T::Id) and Object(Box\<T\>)7. Boxing the Object(Box\<T\>) variant is mandatory in Rust to prevent infinite compile-time struct size recursion—such as an Invoice containing an Expandable\<Subscription\>, which in turn contains an Expandable\<Invoice\>—and to minimize stack frame bloat when moving parent structs across async boundaries5.  
Equally critical is handling Stripe's enumeration policy. As documented in stripe-node, the vast majority of Stripe enums are **open enums**, meaning Stripe can introduce new string values at any time without requiring an API version upgrade, while only a small subset are guaranteed to be closed33. If some-stripe generates standard Rust enum types without a catch-all fallback, any newly introduced payment method type, network code (rtp), or status value from Stripe will trigger a serde\_json deserialization failure in production31. Therefore, all generated enums carry the \#\[non\_exhaustive\] attribute and deserialize unrecognized strings into an Unknown(String) variant33.

### **Auto-Pagination Engine and Concurrency Guards**

stripe-node provides three ergonomics for cursor pagination: for await (const item of list) async iteration, .autoPagingEach(callback), and .autoPagingToArray({ limit })33. This functionality applies not only to top-level .list() calls, but also to nested collection endpoints such as invoices.listLineItems and checkout.sessions.listLineItems5. In some-stripe-core, pagination returns a Paginator\<T, P\> state machine that implements futures\_core::Stream\<Item \= Result\<T, StripeError\>\> alongside convenience methods .auto\_paging\_each(f) and .auto\_paging\_to\_vec(limit)3.  
Implementing this stream in the microkernel requires supporting three distinct pagination envelopes across the Stripe API1:

> 1. **V1 List Envelope (List\<T\>):** Contains data: Vec\<T\>, has\_more: bool, and url: String, where forward pagination extracts the id of the final element in data and issues a subsequent GET request appending starting\_after=\<last\_id\>6.  
> 2. **V1 Search Envelope (SearchList\<T\>):** Used by search endpoints on payment\_intents, customers, invoices, charges, prices, products, and subscriptions; contains data: Vec\<T\>, has\_more: bool, and a next\_page: Option\<String\> opaque cursor token rather than starting\_after1.  
> 3. **V2 List Envelope (V2List\<T\>):** Finalized in stripe-node v23, removes the v1-only object, has\_more, and url properties entirely, relying on data: Vec\<T\>, next\_page\_url: Option\<String\>, and previous\_page\_url: Option\<String\>6.

A vital reliability requirement emerges from stripe-node Issue \#2730 regarding V2ListIterator18. In stripe-node, V2ListIterator initially lacked the promiseCache concurrency guard present in V1Iterator, meaning concurrent .next() invocations while a page transition was in flight triggered duplicate HTTP requests for the same page, yielding duplicated or out-of-order items18. Furthermore, V2ListIterator only attempted a single .next() call after turnPage(), causing an empty intermediate page (data: \[\] with next\_page\_url still populated) to silently truncate iteration18. In Rust, implementing Stream::poll\_next(self: Pin\<\&mut Self\>, cx: \&mut Context\<'\_\>) prevents concurrent .next() race conditions at compile time because poll\_next requires an exclusive mutable reference (\&mut Self). To prevent silent truncation on empty intermediate pages, the Paginator state machine loops internally within poll\_next: if a fetched page yields an empty data vector while has\_more is true or next\_page\_url.is\_some(), it immediately transitions back to the FetchingNextPage state rather than returning Poll::Ready(None)18.

### **Pluggable Transport, Error Taxonomy, and Idempotent Retries**

To support serverless and edge environments (such as Cloudflare Workers or Pages Functions compiling to WebAssembly) as well as deterministic offline request mocking in unit tests, some-stripe-core decouples HTTP execution behind an async HttpClient trait, mirroring Stripe.createHttpClient() and Stripe.createFetchHttpClient() in stripe-node11. Additionally, as hardened in stripe-node v23, if an underlying socket closes prematurely while the response body stream is still being read, the client classifies the failure as StripeError::ConnectionError (StripeConnectionError) rather than StripeError::ApiError (StripeAPIError), ensuring that automatic network retry policies can safely engage6.

| Error Variant (StripeError) | stripe-node Equivalent (Stripe.errors.\*) | Trigger Condition & HTTP Status | Retryable by Default |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| CardError | StripeCardError | HTTP 402 / type: "card\_error" (declines, expired card, invalid CVC, decline\_code)6 | No |
| InvalidRequestError | StripeInvalidRequestError | HTTP 400 / 404 / type: "invalid\_request\_error" (missing params, invalid IDs)17 | No |
| AuthenticationError | StripeAuthenticationError | HTTP 401 / type: "authentication\_error" (missing or invalid API key)39 | No |
| PermissionError | StripePermissionError | HTTP 403 (insufficient permissions or restricted key scope)39 | No |
| RateLimitError | StripeRateLimitError | HTTP 429 / type: "rate\_limit\_error" (rate\_limit or idempotency\_key\_in\_use)38 | Yes (Exponential Backoff) |
| IdempotencyError | StripeIdempotencyError | HTTP 400 / type: "idempotency\_error" (reusing key with mismatched parameters)38 | No |
| ApiError | StripeAPIError | HTTP 500+ / type: "api\_error" or malformed JSON payload on complete response6 | Yes |
| ConnectionError | StripeConnectionError | DNS failure, TLS error, socket timeout, or incomplete response body stream6 | Yes |
| SignatureVerificationError | StripeSignatureVerificationError | Webhook Stripe-Signature missing, HMAC mismatch, or timestamp out of tolerance4 | N/A (Local Validation) |

When maxNetworkRetries is configured above zero, the microkernel automatically attaches an Idempotency-Key: \<uuid\_v4\> header to all outgoing POST requests (unless explicitly overridden in RequestOptions) and retries on ConnectionError, RateLimitError, HTTP 500+ ApiError, or explicit retry headers, reusing the exact same generated idempotency key across all retry attempts of the operation3.

## **Cryptographic Webhook Verification and Event Engine (feature \= "webhooks")**

### **Constant-Time Signature Verification Pipeline**

The webhook engine in some-stripe replicates the exact verification semantics of stripe-node's src/Webhooks.ts while eliminating memory and timing vulnerabilities4. In stripe-node v23, top-level client shortcuts like stripe.constructEventWithoutVerification() were removed to enforce strict encapsulation under stripe.webhooks.\* (constructEvent, constructEventAsync, constructEventWithoutVerification, signature.verifyHeader, and generateTestHeaderString)4. Furthermore, stripe-node PR \#2885 explicitly added validation to reject blank or whitespace-only webhook signing secrets (isBlankWebhookSecret) before any cryptographic computation occurs1.  
![][image2]  
To achieve complete parity with Webhooks.ts in Rust, the verification engine executes a deterministic six-stage pipeline4:

> 1. **Secret & Payload Pre-Validation:** Confirms that the signing secret (whsec\_...) is non-empty and does not consist solely of whitespace (is\_blank\_webhook\_secret); if it contains leading or trailing whitespace, it flags secret\_contains\_whitespace so that any subsequent verification error can alert the developer to potential whitespace corruption1. The function signature accepts the payload strictly as &\[u8\] or \&str, preventing callers at compile time from passing a pre-parsed JSON object whose re-serialization would alter key ordering or whitespace and invalidate the HMAC4.  
> 2. **Header Parsing (parse\_header):** Splits the Stripe-Signature header string by , and splits each segment by \= into key-value pairs4. It extracts the integer Unix timestamp associated with the key "t" and collects all signature hex strings whose key matches the expected scheme ("v1")4. Collecting multiple "v1" signatures into a list is essential because Stripe transmits both the expiring and newly rolled signing signatures simultaneously during secret rollovers4. If the timestamp is missing or unparseable, or if no "v1" signatures are present, the parser immediately returns StripeSignatureVerificationError (which exposes .header and .payload fields directly on the error struct, matching the v11+ stripe-node specification)4.  
> 3. **Zero-Allocation Streaming HMAC-SHA256 (compute\_hmac\_signature):** Initializes an Hmac\<Sha256\> instance keyed with the signing secret bytes3. Rather than allocating a new heap String to concatenate $timestamp.${payload}, the Rust implementation feeds the ASCII bytes of the timestamp, a single literal period byte (b"."), and the raw payload bytes sequentially into the MAC state machine, preventing heap allocation spikes on large webhook payloads4.  
> 4. **Constant-Time Signature Comparison (subtle::ConstantTimeEq):** Each candidate "v1" signature from the header is hex-decoded into a 32-byte array \[u8; 32\] and compared against the computed 32-byte HMAC tag using subtle::ConstantTimeEq::ct\_eq4. Because ct\_eq evaluates fixed-length 32-byte slices using bitwise XOR accumulation without short-circuiting on the first mismatched byte, timing side-channel attacks are completely neutralized, replicating platformFunctions.secureCompare in stripe-node4.  
> 5. **Timestamp Tolerance & Replay Protection Gate:** Once a matching signature is confirmed, the replay protection gate computes the event age ![][image3], where ![][image4] defaults to the current Unix epoch in seconds or an explicitly injected timestamp for deterministic unit testing4. If the configured tolerance is greater than zero (defaulting to 300 seconds) and ![][image5], the verifier rejects the payload with a timestamp tolerance error4.  
> 6. **Test Header Generation (generate\_test\_header\_string):** For unit and integration testing, formats $timestamp.${payload}, computes the HMAC-SHA256 digest, and returns a properly formatted t=\<timestamp\>,v1=\<signature\> header string4.

### **Discriminated Event Unions: Snapshot Events (V1) vs. Thin Events (V2)**

A longstanding ergonomic limitation in stripe-node (tracked in Issue \#758) is that Stripe.Event.Data.Object was historically typed loosely across the \~49 distinct resource objects and \~151+ event type strings, forcing TypeScript developers to manually cast event.data.object as Stripe.Charge or rely on third-party scraped type definitions43. In Rust, some-stripe resolves this natively by generating a strongly-typed discriminated union EventObject keyed off the event's type string—and in keeping with the microkernel philosophy, variants corresponding to disabled domain features gracefully fall back to serde\_json::Value so webhook verification works even on minimal feature builds8.  
Additionally, the event dispatcher supports both **V1 Snapshot Events** and **V2 Thin Events**19. V1 Snapshot Events (/v1/events) embed the complete API resource state directly inside data.object alongside an optional data.previous\_attributes diff map on .updated events19. Developers must account for v1 nuances, such as high-volume events marked *"Selection required"* (which Stripe only emits when explicitly selected on a webhook endpoint rather than via a wildcard subscription) and invoice.upcoming events, which uniquely omit the invoice id field because the previewed invoice has not yet been persisted26. Conversely, V2 Thin Events (/v2/core/events)—designed for high-throughput event destinations including Webhook endpoints, Amazon EventBridge, and Azure Event Grid—transmit only a lightweight notification envelope containing the event id, type, created timestamp, and related\_object reference, requiring the SDK to expose a convenience method (client.v2().core().events().retrieve(id)) to fetch the full resource state on demand1.

| Domain Category | Representative Event Types (EventType) | Embedded data.object Rust Type | Critical Webhook Handling Nuance |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Payments & Intents** | payment\_intent.created, payment\_intent.succeeded, payment\_intent.payment\_failed, payment\_intent.canceled, payment\_intent.requires\_action35 | PaymentIntent26 | Primary fulfillment trigger; replaces legacy charge.\* workflow19. |
| **Charges, Refunds & Disputes** | charge.succeeded, charge.failed, charge.captured, charge.refunded, charge.refund.updated, charge.dispute.created, charge.dispute.closed35 | Charge, Refund, Dispute8 | charge.refund.updated fires on selected payment methods when refund status transitions8. |
| **Checkout Sessions** | checkout.session.completed, checkout.session.expired, checkout.session.async\_payment\_succeeded, checkout.session.async\_payment\_failed35 | CheckoutSession35 | Delayed payment methods (e.g., SEPA, Boleto, Konbini) require waiting for async\_payment\_succeeded before fulfillment21. |
| **Billing & Subscriptions** | customer.subscription.created, updated, deleted, paused, resumed, trial\_will\_end, pending\_update\_applied, pending\_update\_expired35 | Subscription44 | Sub-resource updates (customer.subscription.updated) do not trigger parent customer.updated events26. |
| **Invoices & Recovery** | invoice.created, finalized, paid, payment\_succeeded, payment\_failed, payment\_action\_required, upcoming, voided, marked\_uncollectible, updated44 | Invoice26 | invoice.upcoming has id: None because it previews an uncreated future invoice44. |
| **Customers & Methods** | customer.created, updated, deleted, customer.source.created, updated, expiring, payment\_method.attached, detached, updated, automatically\_updated35 | Customer, PaymentSource, PaymentMethod35 | payment\_method.automatically\_updated fires when card networks push account updater replacements44. |
| **Connect & Applications** | account.updated, account.application.authorized, account.application.deauthorized, account.external\_account.created, updated, deleted, application\_fee.created, refunded, application\_fee.refund.updated26 | Account, Application, ExternalAccount, ApplicationFee, FeeRefund26 | Connect webhooks include a top-level account field identifying the connected merchant account35. |
| **Payouts & Balance** | balance.available, payout.created, payout.paid, payout.failed35 | Balance, Payout35 | balance.available is not emitted for negative balance transactions35. |
| **Apps & Ecosystem** | apps.install.created, apps.install.deleted26 | AppsInstall26 | Sent to app developer, embedding platform, and installing merchant26. |

## **Complete Stripe Service Catalog and Feature-Gated Plugin Specifications**

To guarantee 100% functional parity with stripe-node and stripe-java, some-stripe organizes its resource plugins into three structural tiers mounted onto the microkernel: **V1 Root Core Services** (accessed directly on client.\<service\>()), **V1 Namespaced Product Services** (accessed via client.\<namespace\>().\<service\>()), and **V2 Services** (accessed via client.v2().\<namespace\>().\<service\>())5.

### **Tier 1: Core Payments, Confirmation Tokens, and Payment Methods (V1 Root — feature \= "payments")**

Modern Stripe payment orchestration centers on the PaymentIntent and SetupIntent state machines, augmented by the ConfirmationToken flow22. Rather than passing raw PaymentMethod IDs from the frontend to the server, two-step server-side confirmation flows use Stripe.js (stripe.createConfirmationToken) to bundle payment details (payment\_method\_preview), shipping, mandate\_data (including customer IP and user-agent online acceptance), return\_url, setup\_future\_usage (on\_session or off\_session), and payment\_method\_options (such as card cvc\_token and installment plans: fixed\_count, bonus, or revolving) into a single-use ConfirmationToken (ctoken\_...)20. The backend server inspects this token via GET /v1/confirmation\_tokens/:id to execute validation or tax calculations before passing confirmation\_token to paymentIntents.create or paymentIntents.confirm20. Note that in PaymentIntent, the legacy charges list field was removed in API version 2022-11-15 and replaced with the expandable latest\_charge field32.  
Additionally, some-stripe types all 37+ regional and alternative payment method configurations nested inside PaymentIntent, SetupIntent, ConfirmationToken, and PaymentMethod structs: Cards, ACH Direct Debit, ACSS Debit, Affirm, Afterpay/Clearpay, Alipay, BECS Debit, Bancontact, BLIK, Boleto, Customer Balance, Cash App Pay, EPS, FPX, Giropay, GrabPay, iDEAL, Klarna, Konbini, MB WAY, MobilePay, Multibanco, OXXO, Przelewy24, Pay by Bank, PayNow, PayPal, PayTo, Pix, PromptPay, SEPA Debit, Sofort, Sunbit, TWINT, UPI, WeChat Pay, and Zip21.

### **Tier 4: The 18 Specialized Product Namespaces (V1 Namespaced Microkernel Plugins)**

As highlighted in stripe-node Issue \#2662 and the stripe-java service package index, Stripe isolates 18 specialized product lines into nested namespaces rather than placing their resources directly on the root client5. In stripe-node, a regression in v22.0.0 briefly broke TypeScript exports for nested parameter namespaces (such as Stripe.Checkout.SessionCreateParams.LineItem) across all 18 namespaces5. In some-stripe, each of these 18 namespaces—plus the crypto namespace—maps to an independent, feature-gated Rust module (some\_stripe::\<namespace\>) with public parameter struct re-exports and an individual Cargo feature flag (feature \= "checkout", feature \= "billing", feature \= "treasury", etc.)5.

#### **The TestHelpers Namespace (stripe.testHelpers — feature \= "test-helpers")**

Alongside production product namespaces, stripe.testHelpers provides programmatic simulation endpoints under /v1/test\_helpers/\* so developers can test asynchronous state transitions, time progression, and physical hardware actions in sandbox environments without manual intervention5. In some-stripe, this namespace is gated behind the test-helpers Cargo feature flag so simulation types are never compiled into production release binaries unless requested5.

| test\_helpers.customers | /v1/test\_helpers/customers | fund\_cash\_balance (simulates incoming customer bank transfers to cash balances)14 |
| test\_helpers.issuing | /v1/test\_helpers/issuing/\* | authorizations (create, capture, expire, finalize\_amount, increment, reverse), cards (deliver, fail, return\_card, ship), personalization\_designs (activate, deactivate, reject), transactions (create\_force\_capture, create\_unlinked\_refund, refund)5 |
| test\_helpers.refunds | /v1/test\_helpers/refunds | expire (simulates expiration of an asynchronous refund)5 |
| test\_helpers.terminal | /v1/test\_helpers/terminal/readers | present\_payment\_method, succeed\_input\_collection, timeout\_input\_collection5 |
| test\_helpers.treasury | /v1/test\_helpers/treasury/\* | inbound\_transfers (succeed, fail, return\_inbound\_transfer), outbound\_payments, outbound\_transfers, received\_credits (create with ach, us\_domestic\_wire, or rtp network), received\_debits (create)5 |

### **Tier 5: API V2 Services (stripe.v2 — features \= \["v2-core", "v2-billing", "v2-money-management"\])**

As evidenced by the stripe-node v23 changelog and recent Stripe API documentation, Stripe is actively expanding the /v2/ namespace for high-throughput, next-generation services1. Unlike v1, v2 endpoints use JSON request bodies, operation-specific parameter types, V2List pagination (next\_page\_url and previous\_page\_url), and V2SearchResult envelopes1.

| stripe-node V2 Accessor | Cargo Feature Flag | Endpoint Prefix | Supported Operations & Architectural Role |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| stripe.v2.core.events | v2-core | /v2/core/events | retrieve, list (returns V2List\<V2Event\>; supports thin event lookup and payload hydration)6. |
| stripe.v2.core.eventDestinations | v2-core | /v2/core/event\_destinations | create, retrieve, update, list, del, disable, enable, ping (configures Webhook endpoints, Amazon EventBridge, and Azure Event Grid destinations)30. |
| stripe.v2.core.accounts | v2-core | /v2/core/accounts | create, retrieve, update, close (next-generation unified account & identity model with operation-specific Identity.Individual.Address structs)6. |
| stripe.v2.billing.meterEventSession | v2-billing | /v2/billing/meter\_event\_session | create (generates authentication tokens for high-throughput meter event ingestion)6. |
| stripe.v2.billing.meterEventStream | v2-billing | /v2/billing/meter\_event\_stream | create (high-frequency session-authenticated batch usage ingestion)6. |
| stripe.v2.billing.meterEvents | v2-billing | /v2/billing/meter\_events | create (synchronous v2 meter event ingestion)6. |
| stripe.v2.billing.meterEventAdjustments | v2-billing | /v2/billing/meter\_event\_adjustments | create (cancels erroneous meter events)6. |
| stripe.v2 Money Management & Payouts | v2-money-management | /v2/money\_management/\* | Includes outbound\_setup\_intents, payout\_intents, payout\_methods, payout\_methods\_bank\_account\_specs, received\_credits, recipient\_verifications, and transactions20. |

## **Microkernel Workspace Topology and Implementation Synthesis**

Generating Rust structs, builders, and enum definitions across all 38 v1 core services, 18 v1 product namespaces, v2 endpoints, and 150+ webhook event types produces hundreds of thousands of lines of Rust code8. As demonstrated by the async-stripe 1.0 Alpha overhaul, placing all generated types into a single crate results in prohibitive compilation times and excessive memory consumption during cargo build8. To achieve instant compilation for simple use cases while scaling cleanly to enterprise workflows, some-stripe implements its **Microkernel Architecture** via a multi-crate Cargo workspace re-exported through the top-level some-stripe facade crate8:  
some-stripe/ (Facade Crate — Feature Flags Mount Plugins onto the Microkernel)  
├── crates/  
│ ├── some-stripe-core/ \# THE MICROKERNEL (Zero-Codegen Runtime)  
│ │ ├── client.rs \# Thread-safe StripeClient (Arc)  
│ │ ├── options.rs \# RequestOptions (Stripe-Account, Idempotency-Key, Retries)  
│ │ ├── transport.rs \# Pluggable HttpClient trait (Hyper/Reqwest/WASM Fetch)  
│ │ ├── serializer\_v1.rs \# Indexed-bracket application/x-www-form-urlencoded \+ Nullable  
│ │ ├── pagination.rs \# Paginator Stream (List, SearchList, V2List \+ guards)  
│ │ ├── types.rs \# Expandable, Metadata, RangeQuery, Currency  
│ │ └── error.rs \# StripeError taxonomy & ConnectionError body-read guard  
│ ├── some-stripe-webhooks/ \# CRYPTOGRAPHIC ENGINE (Standalone or Mounted via webhooks)  
│ │ ├── signature.rs \# Streaming HMAC-SHA256 \+ subtle::ConstantTimeEq \+ 300s replay guard  
│ │ └── events.rs \# Feature-aware EventObject discriminated union (V1 Snapshot & V2 Thin)  
│ ├── some-stripe-payments/ \# Plugin: payments, checkout  
│ ├── some-stripe-billing/ \# Plugin: customers, products, billing, billing-portal, entitlements, tax  
│ ├── some-stripe-connect/ \# Plugin: connect, payouts  
│ ├── some-stripe-financial/ \# Plugin: issuing, treasury, terminal, financial-connections, reserve  
│ ├── some-stripe-specialized/ \# Plugin: radar, identity, forwarding, climate, crypto, sigma, reporting, apps, test-helpers  
│ └── some-stripe-v2/ \# Plugin: v2-core, v2-billing, v2-money-management

> 1. **The Microkernel Base (some-stripe-core):** A zero-codegen foundational crate housing StripeClient, RequestOptions, the pluggable HttpClient trait, the v1 bracketed application/x-www-form-urlencoded serializer, the v2 JSON serializer, Expandable\<T\>, Nullable\<T\>, List\<T\>, SearchList\<T\>, V2List\<T\>, V2SearchResult\<T\>, the Paginator stream engine, and the StripeError hierarchy1.  
> 2. **Isolated Cryptographic Verification (some-stripe-webhooks):** Structured as a lightweight, standalone crate depending only on hmac, sha2, subtle, hex, and serde\_json3. Isolating webhook verification allows serverless functions and edge workers to verify Stripe-Signature headers in constant time without compiling the outbound HTTP client when outbound requests are unnecessary, while still re-exporting seamlessly under some\_stripe::webhooks4.  
> 3. **Composable Domain Plugins:** Above the microkernel and webhook crates, the generated OpenAPI domain models are partitioned into logical sub-crates (some-stripe-payments, some-stripe-billing, some-stripe-connect, some-stripe-financial, some-stripe-specialized, and some-stripe-v2), each conditionally compiled and mounted onto StripeClient via Cargo feature flags on the main some-stripe facade crate5.  
> 4. **Automated OpenAPI & stripe-mock Verification:** Finally, the code generation pipeline is pinned directly to Stripe's official OpenAPI specifications and verified in continuous integration against stripe-mock pinned to the exact SDK OpenAPI version (mirroring stripe-node PR \#2870), ensuring that every microkernel serializer rule, pagination guard, and constant-time cryptographic check remains strictly synchronized with upstream Stripe releases1.
